tldr: Gheorghe-Roman shows how a Spring AI agent for military resource allocation runs fully air-gapped: local models behind one ChatClient, self-hosted MCP tools, precise tool descriptions and human approval for writes.
summary: Mihaela Gheorghe-Roman, a senior software architect at Systematic working on a command-and-control platform, describes taking an AI agent to production in a defence network with no internet, no cloud APIs and no external services. Only two people in the room had run an agent unattended in production. Air-gapped means more than pointing an SDK at localhost: no cloud inference, no pulling a newer model (an upgrade can trigger formal re-accreditation), no external registries or SaaS observability, and every dependency must be inside the boundary on day one. She names the category DDIL: disconnected, denied, intermittent, low-bandwidth.

Her simplified scenario: six units across three sectors, a priority-one mission, and an agent recommending allocations. The key decision comes before any code. Reads (unit status, availability, conflict detection) run freely and are logged. Any write that changes state a human must know about, such as reallocating a unit, can only be proposed and must wait for human approval; if in doubt, treat it as a write. Unlike a shopping order, a wrong reallocation cannot be returned. Third-party models like Mistral and in-house ones face the same accreditation; she said Anthropic's terms exclude defence use. The demo uses Ollama with Llama 3.2 as a stand-in.

The architecture is a Spring AI advisor chain (logging, approval, audit), a local chat model behind the provider-agnostic ChatClient, and @Tool methods, some exposed by self-hosted MCP servers owned by other teams. A small local model picks tools only from the description, so she gives a four-sentence docstring: what it returns, when to use it, the ID format, and a negative instruction pointing mission questions to another tool. In the recorded demo, with tools off the agent invents a status for a non-existent unit, Phantom 9; with tools on it says the unit does not exist. The approval demo shows approve and reject; a timeout counts as rejection.
keyPoints: Air-gapped deployment removes cloud inference, same-day model upgrades (an upgrade may require re-accreditation), external registries and SaaS observability; every dependency must be inside the boundary before the mission starts.

Split tools into reads, which run freely and are logged, and writes, which the agent may only propose with prepared parameters; any state change a human must know about is a write, and if in doubt it's a write.
A Spring AI advisor chain wraps each call in a fixed order: logging, approval, audit, with audit recorded on the way out once everything is resolved.
Keep every model behind Spring AI's ChatClient so switching local model profiles or adopting a newly accredited model is a configuration line, not a business-logic change.
Self-hosted MCP servers owned by different teams (units, logistics, intelligence) act as the tool registry; tools wrap existing internal REST services or operational data stores.

A small local model chooses tools only from the description, so write it as a prompt: what it returns, when to use it, the expected ID format, and a negative instruction naming the tool to use instead.

With tool calling off, Llama 3.2 confidently gave a status, location and 92% readiness for a non-existent unit; with tools on it reported the unit was not found. A bigger model does not fix poor descriptions.

Unanswered approval requests time out after a product-defined interval and count as rejections; proposals include a score breakdown and confidence level so the operator can see why the agent suggested them.
takeaways: Classify every agent tool as read or write before writing code, and route all writes through an explicit human approval step.
Rewrite your tool descriptions to state output, when to use, argument format and which similar tool not to confuse it with.
Access models only through a provider-agnostic abstraction such as Spring AI's ChatClient so a model swap is pure configuration.
Decide explicitly whether an approval timeout means reject, and log who approved what, when and why for later reconstruction.
Size hardware for worst-case concurrent load, not for the demo, when running models locally.

quotes.text: If we are in doubt whether it is considered a read or a write, then it's a write operation. It's less risky.
The description field isn't just a code comment, it's the actual prompt.
Local models hallucinate exactly the same way cloud models do. Running on your own hardware doesn't make a model more thoughtful.

watchIf: You build agents for regulated or isolated environments such as defence, healthcare or finance and need a concrete pattern for local models, tool design and human approval of writes.
